column1: What is a consumer-driven contract?
column2: A contract where the client defines expectations and the server implements to meet them. Consumer-driven contracts empower clients to define their needs; providers implement to satisfy the contract.

column1: How do contract tests differ from end-to-end tests?
column2: Contract tests are faster because they focus on API format, not full system behavior. Contract tests validate API format without requiring full service startup. They're faster than end-to-end tests and provide quicker feedback.

column1: What does jsonschema.validate(response, schema) do?
column2: It checks that the response matches the expected schema (required fields, types). jsonschema.validate checks that the response conforms to the schema: required fields are present, types are correct, and no extra fields violate constraints.

column1: Why should contract tests run in CI?
column2: To catch breaking changes before merging, preventing integration failures. Contract tests in CI fail when an API change breaks compatibility, preventing merges and catching issues early before they reach production.

column1: What should happen if a provider contract test fails?
column2: Fix the implementation to satisfy the contract, or update the contract if intentional. A failing provider contract means the implementation doesn't meet the contract. Either fix the implementation or intentionally update the contract (and notify clients).

column1: Time complexity of consumer-driven contract test (client expectations)?
column2: O(1) milliseconds

column1: Time complexity of provider contract test (server behavior)?
column2: O(n) where n is number of scenarios

column1: Time complexity of schema validation (request or response)?
column2: O(n) where n is schema depth

column1: Time complexity of end-to-end test (full client + server interaction)?
column2: O(n) seconds

column1: Time complexity of contract test in CI with multiple consumers?
column2: O(n*m) where n is consumers, m is scenarios per consumer

column1: What is the main difference between unit tests and integration tests?
column2: Unit tests are faster and test components in isolation; integration tests verify interactions between components. Unit tests isolate components; integration tests verify cross-component interactions. Integration tests may use real databases or in-memory replicas.

column1: What does a session-scoped fixture do?
column2: Runs setup once per test session and reuses it across all tests. Session-scoped fixtures run setup once and reuse the result across all tests in the session. This amortizes expensive setup cost but requires careful cleanup.

column1: How does transaction rollback keep database tests isolated?
column2: It reverts all changes after each test, so the database is clean for the next test. A test's writes are wrapped in a transaction that rolls back, leaving the database clean. No explicit cleanup needed; the database is fresh for the next test.

column1: What is a contract test?
column2: A test that verifies a service conforms to its API contract (request/response format). Contract tests verify that both client and server agree on API format (schema, status codes, error messages). Misalignment breaks the contract.

column1: Why might you use a module-scoped fixture instead of a session-scoped one?
column2: Module scope provides finer isolation granularity; setup is shared per module, not per session. Module scope balances speed (reuse setup per module) and isolation (fresh setup for each new module). It's a middle ground between function and session scopes.

column1: Time complexity of integration test (real database, transaction rollback)?
column2: O(n) milliseconds to seconds, depends on database operations

column1: Time complexity of session-scoped fixture (database connection, expensive setup)?
column2: O(1) setup per session; reused across all tests

column1: Time complexity of module-scoped fixture?
column2: O(1) setup per module

column1: Time complexity of function-scoped fixture (cleanup after each test)?
column2: O(n) where n is number of tests

column1: Time complexity of contract test (verify request/response schemas)?
column2: O(1) for each contract assertion

column1: Time complexity of parallel integration tests (pytest-xdist with real database)?
column2: O(n/p) but limited by database connection pool

column1: What is dependency injection in pytest?
column2: Tests declare parameters matching fixture names; pytest injects the fixtures. Pytest uses the test function's parameter names to match fixtures. If a test has a parameter named 'tmp_path', Pytest injects the built-in tmp_path fixture.

column1: What is conftest.py?
column2: A pytest file that defines shared fixtures available to all tests in that directory and subdirectories. conftest.py is a pytest convention; fixtures defined there are automatically discovered and available to all tests in that directory and subdirectories.

column1: How does the `yield` keyword in a fixture work?
column2: It separates setup (before yield) from cleanup (after yield). yield separates setup and cleanup in a fixture. Code before yield runs before the test; code after yield runs after the test, even if the test fails.

column1: What does fixture scope control?
column2: When setup runs and when cleanup happens (function, module, session). Fixture scope determines: function-scoped fixtures run before each test; module-scoped fixtures run once per module; session-scoped fixtures run once per session.

column1: How can a fixture depend on another fixture?
column2: By declaring the other fixture as a parameter. A fixture can take another fixture as a parameter. Pytest resolves the dependency chain and runs setup in order.

column1: Time complexity of simple fixture (no dependencies, function scope)?
column2: O(1) setup, O(1) cleanup per test

column1: Time complexity of session-scoped fixture (reused across all tests)?
column2: O(1) setup once; O(1) cleanup at end

column1: Time complexity of fixture composition (fixture depends on another fixture)?
column2: O(1) per dependency; resolved in order

column1: Time complexity of fixture with monkeypatch (patching module globals)?
column2: O(1) patch, O(1) restore

column1: Time complexity of parameterized fixture (@pytest.fixture(params=[...]))?
column2: O(n) where n is number of parameter values

column1: Why should unit tests avoid calling external services like databases or APIs?
column2: Tests should be hermetic: deterministic, fast, and runnable in any order or location. Hermetic tests are isolated and reproducible. They run in milliseconds, in any order, and don't depend on network or service availability.

column1: Which pytest marker should a fast, isolated test declare?
column2: @pytest.mark.unit. @pytest.mark.unit tags fast, isolated component tests. Markers allow running only unit tests before commit with `pytest -m unit`.

column1: What does unittest.mock.MagicMock.side_effect do?
column2: Raises an exception or returns a value when the mock is called. side_effect can be an exception (raises it) or a callable (calls it). This lets tests trigger error paths without raising real errors.

column1: In dependency injection, what is passed to the function being tested?
column2: A mock object that simulates the service. Mocks replace real dependencies in tests, allowing control over inputs and verification of behavior without side effects.

column1: What does @pytest.mark.parametrize do?
column2: Runs a test multiple times with different inputs. Parametrize runs the same test function with different arguments, specified as a list of tuples. This keeps tests DRY.

column1: Time complexity of unit test (mock dependency)?
column2: O(1) milliseconds

column1: Time complexity of unit test setup (fixture with monkeypatch)?
column2: O(1) setup time

column1: Time complexity of mock assertion (verify call count, args)?
Time complexity of unit test with parametrize (@pytest.mark.parametrize)?
column2: O(n) for n inputs

column1: Time complexity of test collection (pytest discovery)?
column2: O(n) where n is number of test files

column1: Time complexity of parallel unit tests (pytest-xdist, -n auto)?
column2: O(n/p) where p is number of processes
